content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a comprehensive guide titled Planning and Implementing Palliative Care Services: A Guide for Programme Managers. This document provides detailed guidance on organizing and administering palliative care services, including their utilization in various settings such as home-based, community-based, and hospital-based care. It also emphasizes the integration of palliative care into national health systems and highlights its importance as a core component of health planning and national health programs. Palliative care is defined as an approach that enhances the quality of life for patients (both adults and children) and their families who are dealing with life-threatening illnesses. It focuses on preventing and alleviating suffering through early identification, accurate assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychological, social, or spiritual challenges. This care promotes dignity, quality of life, and adaptation to progressive illnesses, using the best available evidence. For children, palliative care involves comprehensive care for the child’s body, mind, and spirit, as well as support for the family, starting from the time of diagnosis and continuing regardless of whether the child receives curative treatment. Globally, palliative care is needed in 40-60% of all deaths, with an estimated 20 million people requiring it in the last year of their lives. However, access remains limited, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, where 78% of those in need reside. For children, 98% of those requiring palliative care live in lowand middle-income countries, with nearly half in Africa. Despite the high demand, only 14% of people needing palliative care at the end of life receive it. Pain management is a critical component, as moderate-to-severe pain affects 80% of patients with AIDS or cancer and 67% of those with cardiovascular or chronic respiratory diseases at the end of life. However, access to opioid analgesics, essential for pain relief, is severely limited in many parts of the world. The guide outlines the essential practices for primary palliative care, which include identifying patients who could benefit, assessing and reassessing their physical, emotional, social, and spiritual needs, and addressing these needs through appropriate interventions. It emphasizes the importance of communication with patients and their families about diagnosis, prognosis, treatment options, and care goals. The guide also highlights the need for a team-based approach involving healthcare providers, social care workers, and volunteers, and stresses that palliative care can be effectively delivered in any healthcare setting, including patients’ homes, even in resource-limited environments. The manual provides a stepwise approach to planning and implementing palliative care services, tailored to the specific needs and capacities of different settings, particularly lowand middle-income countries. The approach is patient-centered, addressing the needs and expectations of patients and their families while considering social and cultural contexts. The guide does not include clinical protocols but refers users to existing WHO resources for pain and symptom management. The WHO reaffirms its commitment to working with member states to make palliative care a reality for everyone, recognizing it as a fundamental human right. The guide is intended for health program managers at national, provincial, or district levels and provides practical options for building and strengthening palliative care services.
